q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Dish rack is called:
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
n: “Bangguerahan” = dish rack. Memory aid: I couldn't confirm the root. The suffix -han marks a place for something, as in lutuan, so it is the place where dishes are kept.

q: What is the vernacular term for Oakum?
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
n: “Estopa” = oakum. Origin: Spanish estopa “tow”, the coarse fibre used to caulk joints. The same term is also used for: Diglead.

q: What is the vernacular term for Septic vault / septic tank?
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
n: “Poso Negro” = septic vault / septic tank. Origin: Spanish pozo negro “black well”, the usual Spanish word for a cesspit.

q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Bath tub is called:
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
n: “Baniera / Banyera” = bath tub. Origin: Spanish bañera “bathtub”, from baño “bath”.

q: What is the vernacular term for Diglead?
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
n: “Tingga, Estopa” = diglead. Origin: tingga is Tagalog “lead”; estopa is Spanish “tow” (oakum). Together they are what is used to seal pipe joints: oakum first, then molten lead. The same term is also used for: oakum.

q: What is the vernacular term for Lavatory?
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
n: “Lababo” = lavatory. Origin: Spanish lavabo “washbasin”, from lavar “to wash”. Related to English “lavatory”.

q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Shower head?
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
n: “Ducha” = shower head. Origin: Spanish ducha “shower”, borrowed from French douche.

q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Sink?
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
n: “Prigadero” = sink. Origin: Spanish fregadero “kitchen sink”, from fregar “to scrub”.

q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Plumbing?
ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
n: “Tuberia” = plumbing. Origin: Spanish tubería “piping”, from tubo “pipe”.
